utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. I ask the Registrar to call out the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-T, Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My name is Mr. Toma Fila, I appear with Ms. Lopicic and Mr. Petrovic for Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me? Before we proceed with our first witness, let me tell you that, on Friday, we had a meeting with the President of this Tribunal and all the presiding judges. We eventually agreed upon the final courtroom schedule for May, June, July and August. As a result of the agreement reached in that meeting, it is now clear that we have two weeks -- we can sit on this case for two weeks in May, the week from 18 to 22 May -- however, I am afraid only from 8.30 to 12.30 in the morning, every morning, for four hours, including the breaks of course, and then the fourth week of May, namely, from 25 to 29 May, we will sit on this case in the morning and in the afternoon. Then we will have to skip two weeks, because we have other cases, and then we can resume our hearings on 15 June until 18 June -- four working days. We very much hope that, in that week in June, we may wind up our case. Probably there will be rebuttal witnesses and I hope we could also have in that week the closing statements of both parties. Do you think we can make it -- four days, morning and afternoon? I know it is very tight, but we should make an effort. Otherwise, we cannot finish in June and in July there are other cases to be heard by this Trial Chamber, so I wonder whether we could really make an effort and finish by 18 June. We very much rely upon the cooperation of both parties. I wonder whether there are any questions relating to this particular point?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it standard procedure, because in my country it is, that the final summing up is given in writing and then is submitted orally, briefly, which makes matters more succinct -- the final argument, is it given in writing first? That is the Yugoslavian system, but it does not mean it is a good one and valid here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It could be quite good. I think this would be a way of saving time, to have the closing statements first in writing and then very briefly summed up orally. Mr. Niemann, would you accept this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We will produce something in writing in the nature of a summary, particularly a directory to the evidence, so that when we say that this element is proved and this is the evidence that proves it, we will be doing something along those lines. We still want to make a closing address, though. It is important I think for this to be orally presented so it can be argued. It also provides an opportunity if there are any questions that occur to your Honours about the Prosecution case or the Defence case, often oral presentation prompts that sort of issue and then your Honours can deal with it. Otherwise, there is this sort of going back and forth on issues which often happens with written submissions. We will be producing something in writing. It will be in the nature of a summary, but we also wish to address you orally on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but I understand this is also what Mr. Fila was proposing -- his idea was, however, that the oral presentation should be fairly short and then followed by questions and the bulk of the argument should be found in the written statement. So, therefore, we could try to have closing statements and oral presentations -- it very much depends on how much time you need for the rebuttal witnesses. We may have only four working days in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not in a position to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But assuming you were to need only, say, two days for the rebuttal witnesses, then we could have two days for closing statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. That would be ample time. I do not imagine I would take anything like a whole day, but I would imagine that I would take three hours for a closing address, and probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, what is the rule about rebuttal evidence? Is it evidence which you were not in a position to call in your evidence-in-chief -- that is certainly the rule that I am familiar with. Is that the rule here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I go on my experience in Tadic, which is all I can do, and I think perhaps that the system that your Honour is used to and the one that I am used to is different to that which prevailed in the Tadic case. My understanding of the practice that operates, for example, in one jurisdiction in the United States is that it seems to be broader than certainly I was accustomed to in terms of the presentation of rebuttal evidence. It strictly follows the traditional approach -- it is only those matters which are raised during the course of the Defence case, but it is different in this sense, that in my jurisdiction at least the Prosecution has a responsibility to, in large measure, anticipate defences in the course of its case and to present its evidence dealing with and addressing those questions in the course of the Prosecution case, and that is not the practice that was followed in the Tadic case. What occurred there was that issues that were raised in the Defence case were dealt with by rebuttal evidence. That is why I raised the matter earlier. I know your Honour comes from a jurisdiction that dealt with the matter differently to the way I am accustomed to. There is this obligation on the Prosecution that exists in the jurisdiction I come from -- it did not exist in the Tadic case. Nevertheless, it is fairly expeditiously dealt with, and it is not a drawn-out process at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If I may interrupt, the difficulty is this: given the tightness of the timetable, and the reason it is tight is because, as you know, Mr. Niemann, there are a large number of other cases waiting to be tried and, therefore, we must try this one expeditiously, and speaking for myself, I would regard rebuttal evidence to be in a fairly narrow compass and no doubt that is the way the Prosecution will approach it -- to deal with purely relevant matters and matters which have not been dealt with or possibly have not been dealt with in the Prosecution case in chief. But it may be this is to anticipate matters. However, I think I should, speaking for myself, say that I would be looking at the matter fairly narrowly and trying to keep it in a short compass.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I specifically and deliberately raised it during the case in chief so that if your Honours had any concern about that, we could discuss it then, because I certainly was concerned about it in the Tadic case when it arose and a more broader view was taken of the issue there. That is one of the reasons I raised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be more sensible to discuss it towards the end of the Defence case when you will know roughly what areas you want to cover? It might be sensible, before you start getting the evidence, to discuss what seems to be relevant and what does not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly, I think that would be helpful. At this stage it is hard for us to predict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I just wanted to point out that I hope it is not a question of giving the Prosecution a second bite at the cherry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, it is not that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Very well. We may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: According to Rule 85, your Honours, of the rights of the Defence to give a reply to the evidence submitted by the Prosecution, and that the Trial Chamber present the evidence asked for -- I do not know that I will have evidence of this kind, but for me to know whether I have them or not, I would like the Prosecution, on time, to tell me which evidence it will be submitting so that, in those four days of May, if I have anything as a rejoinder -- Defence evidence in rejoinder that I prepare it -- four days of June, I am sorry, for the Defence evidence in rejoinder. In order to speed up matters, I have nothing against, as I said at the beginning, having, in the course of May, when I have my Defence turn, every proposal that the Prosecution considers would be useful to propose and present during its Defence time -- during the Defence time and that is not contrary to the Rules along with my agreement. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think by and large we should take up the wise suggestion made by Judge May that, in May, before you conclude your case, we can probably discuss with the Prosecutor the question of rebuttal evidence and see the type of evidence the Prosecutor is prepared to present. We should now move on to our next witness; Dr. Bulajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, there has been a turn about in our agenda -- Dr. Bulajic will be second and the first witness is Mr. Dragutin Antic -- he was to have been second but is the first witness this morning. We informed the Prosecution of this on Friday, of this alteration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. DRAGUTIN ANTIC

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Antic, did you, on 14 January 1998, have talks with the investigator for the Defence, Miroslav Vasic, and on that occasion did you sign a statement that I am going to show you now. Would you please show the statement to the witness? It is in Serbian and has been translated into English. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D34 and the translation is D34A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that the document and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the document, my statement signed by me on 14 January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If there are no objections, I should like to propose that documents D34 and D34A be accepted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you graduate from the Faculty of Machine Engineering in Zagreb in 1973?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 12 April 1973, I graduated from the Faculty of Machine Engineering and Shipbuilding in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you just answer "Yes" or "No" to my questions, please -- the answer to that one was "Yes". Where were you employed in the course of your professional career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 1991, when I left Borovo Naselje, I worked in the Borovo plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1973, until the war broke out, in the region of Vukovar, I worked in the Borovo Cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the cooperative of Borovo means for Vukovar and the Vukovar environment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is the footwear-producing factory company and, for the municipality of Vukovar, it was the basic protagonist of the municipality's development and economy. At the time, it had some 23,000 employees and, of that number, 17,000 workers were from Borovo Naselje, Vukovar and the immediate environs. As I have already said, it was the basic protagonist of the region's development and the economy of the municipality of Vukovar as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many people worked in the company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were from Vukovar, Borovo Naselje and the villages 10 to 15 kilometres away and there were 17,000 employees from this region.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What functions did you perform in the Borovo company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, practically all of them. I, first of all, was in the projects department, then I was the deputy manager of the cooperative, and in a word I went through all the phases, from an engineer to the managerial posts and, happily for me, I also performed another function, by virtue of executive power and authority vested in me in the Borovo company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When and why were you replaced as the second man in charge of Borovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was replaced at the end of June 1991, and the basis for my replacement -- on the basis of the executive board which was nominated by the agency for restructuring of the Republic of Croatia, when the complete management organ of the Borovo company were replaced along with the director-general, Mr. Zdravko Egic and in my assessment, let me say for national reasons and for ethnic reasons, because I was an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who replaced you in your post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The director-general and deputy were members of the Croatian ethnic group and a new executive board was set up by the agency for restructuring, as I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other replacements in the Borovo company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that particular time, there were no more replacements in Borovo, but it was just the intention that the new leadership perform to hand out all the directors of the work organisation's papers, which stated that they would be performing the duties as deputy directors and so on, but, as I left Borovo in August, I do not know whether this was actually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was the criterion for distributing individuals at the highest posts? Was it according to their working ability, or some other criterion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, actually, when I was replaced and when the general manager was replaced, it was not by virtue of their professional ability, but national affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were any of the employees of Borovo company arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were arrests in concrete terms at the end, that is to say on 31 May, the director of production for car tyres, Mr. Milan Miljevic, was arrested. He was physically tortured. On 1 June he was released and there were barricades set up at the time between Borovo Selo and Borovo Naselje and he was maltreated along with his driver, and on 2 July, they intended to arrest the director of the leather footwear factory, Mr. Mirko Vujanovi, who, thanks to me, was taken out of Borovo Naselje and taken by train from Vinkovci to Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there cases when the buildings were mined -- buildings belonging to the Serb population, were they blown up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If you can give us some concrete examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that a cafe bar was blown up, that is to say, a restaurant across the road from the bus station in Vukovar, and I also know that a kiosk where the paper "Politika" was sold was also blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what "Politika" is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a daily newspaper issued by the Politika Newspaper Publishing House and this kiosk sold newspapers coming from Belgrade -- the newspaper Politika. I also know that a restaurant was blown up -- it was a restaurant for the preparation of cold food and snacks, where once again the proprietor was of Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there similar instances; were there instances of killing of Serbs in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of July, I do not know whether it was on 1 or 2 July, a man was killed, that is to say, a worker of an enterprise called Nama, it was a chain of department stores in Vukovar and he worked in the weapons department and he was killed on the threshold of his house on 1 or 2 July -- Mr. Jakovljevic, nicknamed "Drakica". I know that because his child went to school with my own child and that is why I know of that particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was talk of who had killed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was said that the killing, the murder, was performed by the members of the HDZ, but who actually did the killing and in what way I do not really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us something about the atmosphere in Borovo Naselje where you lived at the time, that is to say, the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that the atmosphere from --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From April onwards, the atmosphere was fairly frustrating -- it was tense, because, in the evening hours, at dusk, the extremist members of the HDZ, or in fact -- shot -- there was rifle fire in Borovo Naselje. This led to fear and, of course, people, not only the Serbs but the Croats as well, were afraid of this general state of affairs and this was done by the extremists -- ultra extremists, because this did not suit anybody's purposes, nor did it --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there attempts to solve conflicts peaceably?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were attempts of this kind in February and March. For example, a joint meeting was held at the initiative of the Secretary for National Defence at the time, Mr. Zivko Sekulic, to make a proclamation by which these inter-nationality relationships should be calmed down so as to avoid adverse effects. One of the participants at this meeting was myself and 25 or 30 of us signed this document and this was published in the local Vukovar papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you have to leave Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Borovo Naselje because I felt afraid -- when the situation with the directors and managers of the Borovo company happened, I was afraid, and in actual practice, on 7 August, I used a business trip to Belgrade to leave and I stayed in Serbia -- I remained in Serbia and did not return to Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long have you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known Slavko Dokmanovic from 1990, after the multi-Party elections took place in Croatia -- he was nominated President of the assembly of the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did you start closer cooperation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I began to cooperate closely with Mr. Dokmanovic in 1991, when inter-nationality relationships began to come to a head and barricades were set up and it was difficult for people to come to work because of the barricades and we tried, via the municipality organs, to suggest to the existing Government of the Republic of Croatia to try and calm tensions and to try and establish normal inter-human and inter-ethnic relationships and to ensure production to function normally in Borovo. So my contacts with Mr. Dokmanovic were exclusively of an economic nature from the aspects of business and the normal running of production in the Borovo company. We had no other conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long did you continue contact with Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my relations with Dokmanovic went on up to some time in May, after the ignominious events of 2 May in Borovo Selo. After that, I did not have occasion to meet Mr. Dokmanovic, so somewhere from mid May I went to the Municipal Assembly -- and I contacted --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who did you contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had contacts with his Vice-President, Mr. Vidic -- his nickname was Bili -- and I discussed the problems that were of the same nature as the ones that I had been discussing with Mr. Dokmanovic. So, in practical terms, I talked to Vidic until I was replaced, that is to say, until the end of June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When were you mobilised and in what unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was mobilised on 15 September 1991. I was taken to the Vukovar barracks and, from there, I was taken to a unit, a detachment, the Petrova Gora detachment. Let me just say that as I was previously included in the frameworks of the Vukovar detachment, that is to say, Vukovar's Territorial Defence, in previous years, as a reservist captain, then according to the same initiative I was sent, probably, to that particular detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where was the detachment located and what were your functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The detachment was located in Petrova Gora -- the street's name was Petrova Gora and that is where the detachment takes its name from. My duties were logistics. I was a technician -- my duty was to supply the detachment with food, clothing, fuel, lubricants and so on and so forth. Later on, of course, I did distribute the humanitarian aid that came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under the guard brigades when I came, that is, 1 October, and up to that date, I do not know what the command actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The Guard Brigade belongs to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Slavko Dokmanovic during your stay in Vukovar as a fighter of that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see Mr. Dokmanovic in Vukovar at all. I saw Mr. Dokmanovic on one or two occasions in Erdut, where the Government was stationed of the then Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, and I met him in passing, because I would be on my way to a Ministry to ask for diesel fuel and petrol for the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In going about amassing your supplies, did you visit the farming cooperatives around the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, we used supplies from local sources -- those local sources as far as food is concerned is what we found in Vukovar proper, and the surrounding villages, and of course the farms that were nearby. It was the Ovcara pig-rearing farm and the Jakobovac farm and on these farming cooperatives, so I went there to try and get the necessary meat, whether pork or beef.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At these cooperative farms, did you see any military units stationed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were military units, but how they were deployed, I do not really know, but they were stationed in the environs, because this whole area behind Vukovar -- there were units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there any farming mechanisation on the cooperatives that you visited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did not, to tell you the truth, pay attention to this, but there was the usual farming mechanisation that I saw in peacetime before war broke out, which means tractors and all the other machines, combine harvesters and so on -- other agricultural machines that are used. I did not notice anything different, more or less, that had existed in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there water and electricity in the villages around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let us make a distinction here. Water and electricity, as it once existed in urban terms, that is to say, from the waterworks of Vukovar, taking water to the surrounding villages, the distribution network for electricity, this was not possible at that time for the simple reason that individual power stations and cable units were severed, due to the war activities, and so there was no electricity and, as there was no electricity, the pumps at the waterworks were not functioning. The electricity that we had in Vukovar and the water that we had was from the wells, that is to say, water would be pumped by a hand pump from the wells. As far as electricity that existed, there were power generators at certain locations run on the basis of petrol and so individual buildings had a bit of electricity, but in fact there was no water or electricity. I left Vukovar at the end of January 1992, and I believe that, until April, they had no water or electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just speak a little more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I seem to lose myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the town after the war operations, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Throughout the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During the war operations and later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was military rule, particularly afterwards, when the war operations had ended and when the Guard Brigade had withdrawn, then the military authority was taken over by the Kragujevac Brigade. The commander was Colonel Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he came --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is alright, yes, he came after the war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When the Guard Brigade had withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, somewhere between 24 and 26 November. I do not know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any civilian organs of power and authority in the Vukovar region after the war operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the war operations -- that is to say, during the war operations, there was no civilian authority. Civilian authority began to be set up at the beginning of December 1991 and the military government had as its task to enable the creation of normal living conditions, and to prepare new organs of civilian government and to enable those who had fled Vukovar and Borovo Naselje and the surrounding villages to return. All I know is that some time at the beginning of December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you to slow down, otherwise the interpreters cannot interpret what you say. Thank you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: President, I have to apologise. I simply seem to lose myself. Let me just finish what I set out to say. So the civilian authorities were non-existent, the military rule was supposed to solve this problem and then, in early December, the Executive Council of the Municipal Assembly was formed. It had five members and I remember that the President was Mr. Rade Bibic -- he was appointed the President. I cannot tell you anything more about that because I did not participate in that and I did not know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What happened to your property and the property of other people who left Vukovar and the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as my property is concerned, two things happened. On the one hand, in July, when the first onslaught was happening, the National Guard Corps, the Croatian ZNG, entered my house, because they thought I had weapons and they destroyed all my furniture, so that I could not use it any more that was one of the reasons that I had fled. The second thing that happened in the course of the combat operations, due to bombardment and shelling, a part of my property was destroyed, so I lost about half of my property through looting and just the other half I lost through bombardment, and the other inhabitants of Borovo Naselje and Vukovar shared my fate and of the surrounding villages, so those people who were affected by the war operations and, those who did not, did not suffer that fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This concludes my examination of Mr. Antic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that the Government was in Erdut -- you said that a moment ago; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Government -- I mean the appropriate Ministries and the Government, they sometimes met in Erdut and, from time to time, I went there in October 1991. To be more specific, I was there once or twice at the most -- I cannot give you an exact number of times -- and the reason why I went there was to ask for assistance to be given -- I do not know from which sources -- some diesel fuel, because we needed it for the vehicles we had, most of all for the medical vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the supplies that you were seeking were provided by the Government, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, the Government never provided any supplies, but I applied to the appropriate Ministries in the Government to get me in touch with somebody -- some humanitarian organisation -- which would then provide the resources that I needed, that I sought. For instance, if we are talking about -- if there was a company which was under their jurisdiction, or if it was a company in the Republic of Serbia, then I tried to solve the problem in this way. They put me in touch with those people, I talked to these people, and I asked them to donate those resources for free, because we did not have the funds to buy those things, and this is the way I proceeded, so I only went there a couple of times -- this is not something that we should be talking about, because we are not talking about huge quantities. I mostly tried to solve those problems from local resources, because there were some local resources left, but there were times, for instance, in late October, when the local resources were insufficient, because we had already used them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You saw Mr. Dokmanovic when you were seeking these supplies -- seeking to obtain these supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Mr. Dokmanovic at that time there, because Mr. Dokmanovic was the Minister of Agriculture, so I did not have anything in common with him -- we just met in passing, shook hands and said "hello" as people who had known each other. I did not have any other activities or contacts with Mr. Dokmanovic. This is all that I had with him, maybe a second or two -- "Good afternoon, how are you? What are you doing" -- nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As Minister for Agriculture, he was one of the Ministers who was able to put you in touch with people with supplies such as diesel and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he probably could, but I did not ask him to do so, nor was that my intention when I went there. I never discussed those things with Mr. Dokmanovic. I really did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said you discussed these things with the Government and Mr. Dokmanovic was in the Government. Tell me who it is that you had your discussions with -- which Ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alright. That was not your question. I will now give you an answer. At that time, I talked to Mr. Devetak, Vitomir Devetak. I discussed the possibility of obtaining such assistance from him. He was in the Ministry of Industry or something like that, and I discussed those things with him, so I was there where he was and I discussed those things with his associates. I pursued those avenues of obtaining assistance, so, please, at that time, I only said "hello" to Mr. Dokmanovic as a friend -- by a "friend" I mean we knew each other from Vukovar. I had not known Mr. Dokmanovic until the time when he was appointed the President of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You also said in your evidence that towards the middle to late 1991, there was an increase in tension in the "inter-nationality relationships". Can you just tell me what it is you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not until mid 1991 -- until the end of 1991, this resulted in armed hostilities, but the tensions began in 1990. They began to crop up at the time when multi-Party elections were being prepared in Yugoslavia. There were parties which had a nationalist programme and this has caused increased inter-ethnic tensions. I do not know what the previous witnesses have said -- I do not know how familiar you are with the situation, but in May 1990 the elections took place and, as far as our municipality is concerned, there were two basic parties -- two main parties, the Croatian Democratic Union and the former Party of Democratic Changes, that is Racan's Party and in the municipality of Vukovar we had only two options -- either to vote for HDZ or for the Party of Democratic Changes. I have to tell you that most of the Serbian population voted for the Party of Democratic Changes because there was no alternative and also some of the people who in that people were, so to speak, of Yugoslav orientation, they also voted for that Party. The reason for that was simply that some of the people who were involved in the Croatian Democratic Union Party overly stressed this national motive and by stressing that motive, they implied something else -- the other side -- and the result was a contradiction to those people who stressed something else, because we in Borovo Naselje, we all lived side by side for years, we were neighbours, people of all nations and religions until that time when that happened and until that time nobody asked other people what their nationality was. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. I think your point is that the HDZ represented people of Croat nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, that is not what I said. I just wanted to say that, to me, it was not clear why, within the HDZ Party, there were some extremists who created this tension among us, and that was the reason why, in February and March, we had this joint meeting where intellectuals tried to calm down those nationalist passions, in a way, because, as soon as one side started to express their nationalist feeling, the other side also responded. I cannot give you a better explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But there were people of extreme nationalist views on either side, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course -- on the Serbian side I have to say that, but normal human beings could not accept such nationalist motives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The brigade that was at Petrova Gora, was that Territorial Defence, or was that JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time, it was not a brigade; it was a detachment -- we called it the Petrova Gora detachment. At the time when it was formed, established, it had about 400 people. It was under the command of the JNA, and I cannot treat it as being part of the Territorial Defence, so, according to the conception -- I have now to give you an explanation -- according to the conception of All People's Defence, the Territorial Defence was part of the normal armed forces. It was a constituent part, so both the Regular Army and the Territorial Defence were treated -- if there was an attack, it had to defend the country. That was the doctrine and, before the war, I was the chief of the technical service in the Vukovar Brigade, so it was a territorial unit. What that means is that according to some military aspects, it had to be stationed in Vukovar, and it does not mean that it was a paramilitary unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I did not suggest for one minute --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I did not suggest it was a paramilitary unit. The command of the Petrova Gora detachment or what ultimately it became was -- the ultimate command was the same command as the command of the Guards' Brigade; that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The command of the Guards' Brigade was located in Negoslavci -- that is where the headquarters were located, and the commands of the detachment -- the command did not exist in Vukovar, in practical terms. You knew who was the commander of a company. I was in charge of providing supplies, fuel, lubricants, food, footwear, for the soldiers -- I had to prepare places where those soldiers could have baths and where they could be fed, but the command was not there -- the command was in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was not ask you where the command was, I was asking you what the ultimate command was. There is a confusion. I did not suggest they were at Petrova Gora. I am just saying your ultimate command came under the command of the Guards' Brigade -- that is what you said in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right -- the Petrova Gora detachment had a command. Our command was in Vukovar, but we were under the command of the Guards' Brigade. The command of my detachment had to be stationed somewhere -- their headquarters was in the Petrova Gora street. I do not know, Mr. Prosecutor, maybe I do not understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you do not understand what I am saying. I am not asking you about locations; I am asking you about command and you have answered my question, so we can move on. The commander of the Guards' Brigade was commanded by Colonel Mrksic and Major Sljivancanin, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, so that is what you are asking. There has been a misunderstanding. The commander of the Guards' Brigade was Colonel Mrksic, that is right and Lieutenant-Colonel Sljivancanin, I do not know what he was, because I was not in touch with them. I think he was in charge of security, because we did not get into contact. I just know that he was my commander in chief -- my superior officer. If that is what you wanted to ask me, that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did you know other commanders who were operational at the time, and, firstly, commander -- Captain Miroljub Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujovic, yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have much contact with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did have some contact with him, because I supplied his unit with food, and clothes, footwear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was he on a parallel level of rank with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time, he was a commanding officer of a unit -- I do not know whether he was at the parallel level with me -- I do not know. We probably were, because I was in charge of logistics and he was in charge of a combat unit, so we probably were at the same level, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, like you, he was also subordinate to the Guards' Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- well, all the units that operated in Vukovar were subordinated to the Guards' Brigade command -- whether we are talking about the Petrova Gora detachment, the 2nd, 4th, 5th detachment, it does not matter, all of them were subordinate to that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Stanko Vujanovic, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him, he was a commander of a unit, a combat unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Similar to the situation that Miroljub Vujovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Miroljub -- yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Stanko Vujanovic was also subordinate to the Guards' Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of them were subordinate to that Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever have any discussions with either Stanko Vujanovic or Miroljub Vujovic on or after 20 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, virtually after the end of the war operations in Vukovar, I was not in touch with them any longer, because, after that, pursuant to a decision of the military administration, I was assigned to go back to the Borovo company and to take over, so, in fact, in that period, when a commission was formed to clean up the entire area after the war operations, I worked with that commission and I also prepared the Borovo company for the clean-up and for renewal of the production, so I was no longer in Vukovar after 24th -- on 25 November -- I was only in Borovo company and in Borovo Naselje and I stayed in that region until mid January 1992, when I left the region and I never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was it -- you said that it was pursuant to a decision of the military administration that caused you to go back to the Borovo company. Can you be more precise and tell me who it was that gave you that order -- who was responsible --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the order was issued by the commander of the Vukovar town, Mr. Milorad -- I think he was a colonel by rank -- Milorad Vujnovic. He came there as part of the Kragujevac Brigade and it was probably according to the military formation he was put in charge of the town and he gave me this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that Rade Bibic was appointed President of the Executive Council of the municipality of Vukovar. Was Miroljub Vujovic that we spoke of a moment ago also appointed to the Executive Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Executive Council -- yes -- it was some kind of initial council which was supposed to set up all those civilian authorities -- I know about Mr. Bibic, I know there were five members but I do not know who were the other members aside from him, because I was not there at the time, and I did not take part in all that. I do not know whether Miroljub was a member or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a few questions. First of all, I would like to point out that in the English translation of your written statement, which has been admitted into evidence, there is a printing mistake on the penultimate line -- it should read "January 1992", and not "1991". My first question relates to what you said a few minutes ago. You said that you saw military units stationed around Vukovar after you were mobilised for the JNA, and my question is as follows: what sort of military units were these ones -- are you referring to JNA units, or, also, paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in my opinion, these were the units of the JNA, but I really did not check -- I did not check which units they were. My role was to provide supplies and, as far as Ovcara was concerned, there was a pig-breeding farm there and I went there to see whether I can obtain some pork, whether they can kill a pig or two so I can provide food for the people I was supposed to supply, and I know that there were some units there, I suppose it was the JNA, because there was also some artillery station there. It was not possible for some other units to be there -- it was only the JNA, because nobody else had that kind of weapons. That is my assumption, my opinion. It does not mean that it was in fact true, but, in my opinion, it cannot be any other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So, in the three months when you were there you never came across military units dressed in a different way from the normal uniform of JNA units -- namely, paramilitary units, people who were a bit different from the JNA regular members -- you never saw such paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not in essence, because everybody was dressed in the kind of uniforms that the JNA had, so there were not people dressed in any other way. If somebody was mobilised, then they were not given the uniform at that very moment when he was mobilised but only when he came to Vukovar, then he got his uniform in Vukovar. I gave him the uniform there, out of our warehouses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: When you speak of being "mobilised", are you also referring to members of the so-called Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean all those who received their call-ups and members of Territorial Defence and those who were in regular military units -- those who were drafted in the army at that time -- that is what I mean. According to the doctrine at that time, it was one and the same -- there was no difference -- Territorial Defence and regular armed forces, it was one and the same. There was no difference. The name "Territorial Defence" was applied, because that unit was supposed to stay in its territory. If we are talking about the Vukovar Brigade, for instance, and if there are combat operations, the Vukovar Territorial Defence has to remain in the Vukovar municipality. It cannot be deployed in other areas -- Vinkovci, Nasice, Zupanja -- whatever. In those areas, there were brigades which belonged to that territory. According to the doctrines that were valid at that time, they were all armed forces units and the question is only when they were mobilised. They all received their call-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A different question. You said that you went a couple of times to Erdut in October 1991 to meet members of the Ministry of Industry and you also saw Mr. Dokmanovic. You spoke of "Ministries". Could you explain what Ministries these were -- did each Ministry have a building with staff, with people -- a sort of administrative chain of command, so that the Minister would issue orders to his staff and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I am not going to be able to explain some things as well as I should like -- not because I do not want to, but because I was not acquainted with the set-up. But, at the time, there was a Government of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem which, within its frameworks, had the corresponding Ministries. What competencies the Ministries had compared to the Yugoslav People's Army and whether it had any competencies at all, I do not know -- I do not think it had any competencies, any authority, because, in fact, when they wanted Ministers in the Government to undertake an action with the military organs, they were just dead letter on paper, nobody recognised them at all and this is what happened in Vukovar -- everything that happened and everything that was done was exclusively under the direct jurisdiction of the Guard Brigade. It was the Brigade which, in practical terms, did all the commanding for the war operations as well and it received orders from above -- whether it did or did not I do not know, because I was too far down on the ladder to know things of this kind and to be told of things like this. In the Ministries that I went to, that is, that particular Ministry, it was the Ministry of Industry, I went to that Ministry to ask for aid and assistance and to ask for their suggestions as to who would be able to give me the material I needed, but I just happened to meet Mr. Dokmanovic in passing. I did not ask him what his functions were, but I was told that he was Minister of Agriculture at the time, so, by virtue of my post and functions in Vukovar, I had no common points with Mr. Dokmanovic -- we just met as good friends, we shook hands, asked each other how we were, and that was all. So, if I was in Erdut for two or three times, of that two or three times, I probably met Mr. Dokmanovic once or perhaps twice. I cannot really answer you, because six or seven years have gone by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question: when you met Mr. Dokmanovic in Erdut, how was he dressed -- was he wearing a suit, like the one you are now wearing, or what sort of clothes was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I just cannot remember. I think he was wearing the clothes that everybody else was wearing -- whether he had a military or a civilian uniform, I do not really know -- I just cannot remember that detail. I cannot give you an answer to that question -- I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Talking about uniforms, when you yourself were in charge of supplies, as you say, what uniform were you wearing during your duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A military uniform, the uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army, and all the insignia belonging -- the rank of captain, as I had in peacetime, because I am a reserve captain, according to military hierarchy, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: To go back to a question I put about the clothes Mr. Dokmanovic was wearing, would you say that, if he was wearing a military uniform, this would have struck you, because, as a civilian, a member of a Government, Minister of Agriculture, he was probably not expected to wear a military uniform, so in a way, although you said you cannot remember, probably is it a fair assumption to say that, had he worn a military uniform, this would have struck you as something a bit odd -- a member of a civilian Government wearing a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really cannot give you an answer to that question, but, at that particular time of the war operations, most people were wearing military uniforms. Now, whether Mr. Dokmanovic, on that particular occasion, was wearing a uniform or civilian clothing, I just cannot say. There are details that you do not focus on at times like that. I could not expect a question like that, because I never thought about it. If you were to ask me what somebody who was with me in Vukovar was wearing, I probably would not be able to give you an answer there -- they are details you just do not focus on at the time. I am sorry, but I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any further questions? I assume there is no objection to the witness being released? Mr. Antic, thank you so much for coming here to give evidence. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you calling Mr. Bulajic? While we are waiting for him, let me again stress that, since he is not a fact witness but an expert witness and we have already been provided with a written statement on the historical and psychological reasons for the political behaviour of Serbs in Croatia, I think we should not spend too much time on this particular testimony, because, judging from what he put on paper, this is material which we have already heard many times -- these are things which we have heard. I hope that he will give concise answers. I will ask him to be very short in his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am responsible for my own questions and they will be short and precise. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you to stand up and make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Dr. Bulajic, before we start, may I ask you to be so kind as to be short, to give short answers to the questions of the Defence counsel and afterwards of the Prosecutor -- very short answers, thank you. Mr. Fila? DR MILAN BULAJIC

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Bulajic -- sit down, please -- you can switch to channel 6. Are you sitting comfortably, may we begin? Good morning. Did you graduate from the faculty of law in the Higher School of Journalism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you write a doctoral thesis under the title of, "The Rights of People to Self-Determination"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you in the diplomatic service of the SFRY from 1949 to 1987?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you the main legal adviser to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where did your functions outside Yugoslavia within the diplomatic service take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I went to Washington in the United States of America. I was the Secretary of the Embassy and legal adviser. I was then posted to Indonesia, a Minister-Counsellor was my position there. Thirdly, I was the Consul-General in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As a recognised legal man, were you a member of the Federal Council for Legislation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As well as the president of the Yugoslav Association for the Protection of Intellectual Property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- and I am so today.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: A member of the Executive Board of the International Association for the Protection of Industrial Property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you a member of the Executive Committee of the World Association for International Law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you the main rapporteur of the International Committee for the Legal Aspects of the New International Economic Order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you the second vice-president of the Organisation of World Peace through Law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you the deputy president of the Committee of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences for collecting information on the genocide against the Serbian people and other nations of Yugoslavia in the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you Secretary of the State Commission for War Crimes and Crimes of Genocide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you now hold the post of Director of the Museum of the Victims of Genocide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you are President of the Fund for Research into Genocide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you the amicus curiae of the Yugoslav Government at the trial of Eichmann in Jerusalem in 1961?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you an observer of the Yugoslav Government at the trials of Ustashi for attacks on the Yugoslav military mission in West Berlin in 1970?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And, also, at the trial of the Ustashi killers of the Yugoslav Ambassador, Mr. Rolovic, in Stockholm in 1971?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you take part at the trial, as an observer, of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences and the Yugoslav Government for the Andrija Artukovic case, one of the men in Zagreb, and on behalf of the Yugoslav Government did you take part in discussions on the extradition of Artukovic in America before the court in South California of the United States of America in 1958?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Among others, did you publish the following scientific works: "Ustashi Crimes of Genocide and the Trial of Andrija Artukovic in 1986"; "The Jasenovac Myth of Franjo Tudjman"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "Jasenovac: What Happened"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "The Genocide Against the Orthodox Serbs and Other Nations in the Second World War"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "The System of Untruths in the System of Genocide"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "The Destruction of the Yugoslav State, Crime against Humanity and International Peace"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: "The Mission of the Vatican to the Independent State of Croatia", "The Crime against Peace: The Case of the Former Yugoslavia", "The Right to Self-Determination and the United Nations"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this your curriculum vitae and your bibliography?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically, yes -- among others, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: (Handed). Would you take a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D35.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this your expert report, the one that you submitted in English and, on the back, in Serbian? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D36 and the translation D36A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, I should like to ask the Tribunal to accept this as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Bulajic, we have studied your expert report, both the judges, the Defence and the Prosecution and myself, so we will dwell on it briefly. Will you tell us, in brief, by one definition, what the system of Ustashi Jasenovac death camps in fact is -- in a sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try. The system of Croatian Ustashi death camps, in which Jasenovac is just one example, one of the death camps, about 210 to 240 square kilometres of mass graves, in which, in the most brutal manner possible, a genocide was performed by the same perpetrators, on three occasions, which is a world phenomenon, over Orthodox Serbs, Jews, gypsies or Romanies and is the most serious war crime over anti-fascists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to ask the Chamber to show a film now -- the intent of the Defence is that everything you saw in the introduction -- you heard in the introduction, should be seen on the screen so that it would have the value and weight of evidence, if you agree. May we see the film about Jasenovac? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like this film to be a Defence exhibit -- it will be shown in May in extenso and it will be lasting for about 40 minutes. We are just now showing this particular segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am not sure of the relevance of this to this particular case. If Mr. Fila could explain how it is relevant to the issues before this court, we may not have any objection, but we do have concerns; number 1, about the commentary which is offered in connection with it and, number 2, just primarily as to its relevance to the matter before the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, I also had the same misgivings or doubts. Could you explain to us why this film would be relevant to our trial? This is part of history -- what happened in Jasenovac was part of history. I do not know whether and to what extent it is material to our trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, first, I listened to expert Dr. Mark Wheeler, who explained the settlement of the Serbs in the 17th century, and this, according to the Prosecutor, was very important for this case. The Prosecutor provided you with ethnic maps -- Croatian ones -- dating back to the 17th century. There were also population migrations, the relationship between the number of Serbs and number of Croats in this century and this was submitted as evidence. In the written expert report of this witness, the reason is explained for the existence of this particular material as a basis for the Serbs' fear in 1991, and from the questions that I shall be asking subsequently, you will see how important this is for the insecurity that the Serbs felt in the region in 1991 and their reasons to rebel against the Croatian forces; because they were afraid that what happened in 1941 would be repeated. From my next question, you will see how many people from Vukovar left their lives there and we are discussing Vukovar in the 20th century. So, the question is highly relevant, if you wish to learn why the Serbs rose up in 1991. Mr. Wheeler also told you that the fact -- and let me remind you of his statement, a catharsis of the Croatian people did not come about and nobody was punished for those crimes, creating a feeling of additional insecurity in the Serb population and please, I should like to draw attention to the Wheeler expert report, which is the Prosecution's evidence and that is why I am bringing this up -- Jasenovac has been brought up and it was contained in Dr. Wheeler's statement as well as the constitution and so on and so forth, so we must explain and know why the Serbs felt so insecure in 1991. That is the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If I might address a couple of points, briefly. First of all, the Prosecution did not tender any maps anywhere near the 17th century. I am looking at the list of Prosecution exhibits. We tendered a map of the territorial distribution of Serbs in Croatia in 1981, and a "Times" map of the Balkans, which is a current map. The questions that were put to Mr. Wheeler, at the request of your Honours to keep it concise, started with the end of World War II and the formation of Yugoslavia. It was only on cross-examination that Mr. Fila then went back to the 14th century and introduced these whole subjects. It was designed only to give a brief historical perspective as to how Yugoslavia was formed, thus to put it in the context of the break-up, but the Prosecution did not enter into any questions or try to elicit information from this far back in history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Williamson. My own position, but I will consult with my fellow judges, is that of course it is useful to the court to have a very general picture of the historical background, yes, but very general. The question we are now in a way discussing is the amount of evidence you intend to produce on the historical and political background. This has very little relevance to our particular case, which is a case where we deal with the facts and legal issues, so therefore you must be aware of the degree to which we can go -- the extent to which we can go in accepting evidence. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Although we very much doubt the relevance of discussions or films on a period which is far away from the date we are concerned with, namely, 20 November 1991, we do allow you to admit this film into evidence, but with a strong appeal that you should try, as much as possible, to confine yourself to dealing with matters which are material to our case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be marked D37.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I did not consider the Defence represents this as an illustration of what had happened in the sense that you asked for. I am just going to show you some books from that particular area, once again in the sense of illustration, for the purposes of illustration along with the film. As the director of the museum, you wrote a book about how many children lost their lives there, with the names and surnames -- is that the book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to tender this -- the book just contains the names and surnames of the children who were killed -- of all three nations, Serbs, Jews and gypsies. This is an illustration along with the films -- a supplementary illustration to back up the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The Prosecution would have the same objection to these materials as well. Unless this is being offered to show -- as a justification for killings in 1991, then perhaps we would have no objection, but if this is just being provided as historical perspective, again we lodge the same objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am not here to justify killings; I do not like murders of anyone, your Honours. I cannot justify the murdering of Indians, just as much as I cannot justify the killings of Jews and Serbs. No murder is a good thing and it cannot be justified, so I never want to tender into evidence anything that would serve as a justification for murder. This is just an illustration of something that left its trace in the Serbian people and in this spirit it is tendered, to make you understand better the events in 1990 and 1991, the fear that was there. The last thing that I want to tender as supporting material is again a finding of the Academy of Sciences with the list of everything that happened there. Is this a book published by the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Again, I apologise for adding on one more time -- in relation to our objection, also it goes to the fact that if this material is admitted, it certainly broadens the area which we have to cross-examine on. If this is going into evidence, then I think we are going to feel obligated to have to try to counter it to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just add -- (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In light of the objections made by the Prosecutor and, also, because the court strongly feels that all this material is hardly relevant to the case, we cannot allow your admission into evidence of this list of names and so on. So, it will not be admitted into evidence. I wonder whether you could -- we could have a break now, because we -- and resume in 20 minutes. We stand adjourned. (10.10 a.m.) (A short break) (10.35 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Bulajic, you will answer very briefly to my questions, please. Were there victims from Vukovar in Jasenovac, because we are interested in the Vukovar area -- briefly, how many, what happened, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, the distinguished Prosecutor raised the question as to the documents and how far this was justified in light of the latter-day victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What you have in mind is a more lengthy answer, but it is connected to Vukovar; were there victims from Vukovar, and how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were and that is a very important factor. The first composition was made out of five wagon loads of women and children and there were wagon loads of males on 26 August 1941 from Vukovar. It set out for Jasenovac on 27 August 1941, a train composition of 21 wagon loads, two days and two nights travel to Jasenovac, and was liquidated at Gradina. There is a document which I have personally seen, 141 individuals, amongst which were 24 children. There are facts and figures which state that gypsies -- Romanies from the Vukovar area were sent to Jasenovac -- 1,120 adults and 500 children. The first great arrests of the Jews in the Vukovar region took place on 7 November 1941; lists exist with 61 Jews in Jasenovac and the last group of Jews were sent to Jasenovac from the Vukovar area on 26 July 1942.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What were the total number of Jews liquidated in Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to data that I received from Jad Vashem, a photocopy of the highest leadership sent to President Tudjman himself, they remind him that, in Jasenovac, in the most brutal possible way, 25,000 Jews were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. These criminals from Jasenovac, were they punished after World War II in Communist Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, the basic problem as I see it and the cause of the present tragedy of the Yugoslavia peoples, lies in the fact that the Ustashi genocidal State, the independent State of Croatia, did not perform de-Nazification, as was carried out in Germany. The Ustashi terrorist organisation, as was the case with the Nazi Party in Germany, was not proclaimed a criminal Party and that is at the root or heart of matters. The leader of the Ustashi independent State of Croatia fled by rat channels and he was never brought to trial. I was the official observer of the Academy of Sciences at the Andrija Artukovic case, which was to have been a belated Yugoslav Nuremberg trial and I was to have written four books in 3,500 pages to prove that this was a case in pre-war Yugoslavia which was completely staged. The Museum of the Victims of Genocide, whose director I am, along with cooperation by the Wiesental Centre -- Mr. Simon Wiesental -- discovered a live commander of Jasenovac, Dinko Sakic. He is still alive, living in Argentina. He has been living there since 1947 and there is numerous evidence against him. I would like to especially state that, luckily, if I can use that word, there are living witnesses -- people who saw this particular commander of Jasenovac, living in Argentina today, kill the victims personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I must object. We are getting into discussions of individual cases of perpetrators from Jasenovac and I hardly see how that is relevant to our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I shall be concluding with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether the witness could confine himself to specific cases -- not to trials, but general matters we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. In the course of the post-war period in Yugoslavia, was there somebody who went to apologise to the Serbian victims -- was there a Willy Brandt of that people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. I must say, first of all, that neither the President of Yugoslavia, Josip Broz Tito, himself never visited Jasenovac and that the present President of the Republic of Croatia, historian Dr. Franjo Tudjman, apologised on several occasions to the Jews, but he never offered his apologies to the mass of Serb victims, and he never, which is more important, ever mentioned the gypsies, Romanies, who were killed in the most brutal way possible in the Jasenovac camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did this destruction of the Serbs in Jasenovac and the fact that this went unpunished, did it affect the Serbs' behaviour in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the sense of the whole thing. We must look at the roots of the present ills. We said that no de-Nazification had taken place. However, what began to happen before the break-up of the Yugoslav State was that Serbian houses began to be set alight on Croatian territory and what is essential here is that those houses were set aflame in areas where there were no armed conflicts. Therefore, there was a clear orientation towards the cleansing -- towards finishing what had been started in World War II, where the area of Croatia was to have been ethnically cleansed and become a cleansed State. People were being recalled in the militia and the police, people were relocated, towns in Croatia from Zagreb to Rijeka were cleansed of the Serb population and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before this, we come to 1990 and 1991, which are the years you speak about, there was a period in the history of our State which was called the Maspok, or the Croatian Spring of 1968-71. Does this period or movement -- did it have an effect on the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a good question. At that particular time, I was present at the trial of the killers of the Yugoslav Ambassador in Stockholm and I was personally acquainted with the fact that at that time links had been established between the Ustashi terrorist organisations and this new movement, which rose up in Croatia, because it reflected a certain continuity in the fact that pure Croatian States should be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the course of 1990 and 1991, what was Croatian policy like towards Serbia -- towards the Serbs? I am going to show you several films now, which I used in my introduction, and for which the President has asked me where I came by those films, so you can take a look and tell me who gave me the films. They are films used in the Defence's introduction -- opening statement. It spans 1990 and 1991 and I hope that this refers to this particular case. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Remember Vukovar. Death to the Serbs. (Videotape stopped)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is part of the film. What is this about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are the crimes that were ascertained in 1990 and 1991 as Secretary of the State Commission for War Crimes and Genocide and later, as the director of the Museum of Genocide, we created a video film centre -- documents -- on the genocide and war crimes if future generations might need documents of this kind, or this esteemed court.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So, this is a segment of that tape and you gave me the tape; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. May this be tendered into evidence, the tape that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D40 is the number of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May we have the next tape? It is one tape with the different segments. They all refer to the same period -- 1990 and 1991 -- short, brief segments. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please stand up in line, commanders. Line up, please. Cipa, are you there? Line up, please, all of you. Where's Maric? Maric is at the end here. I have already handed all mine over. May I have a little silence, please? According -- by orders of the President of the Republic of Croatia, we must set up -- come on, line up, please. A little silence. By order of the President of the Republic of Croatia, we are forming unarmed detachments. You must know what we are dealing with here. We have received orders to collect the best people who we are going to put forward for the Ministry of Internal Affairs. You know the procedure for that. Who is on the list will go with us, but we must form broader detachments. Next time, we are going to set up the medical corps attached to our detachments. We have 30 per cent of the people here who are possibles. That means that we must now inform them of the command that is going to be up at Graz and Bogdanovci.
