We are going to inform them all why we have gathered here and anybody who is suspect, anybody of shady character should be made a note of. I think we should wait for five minutes to check all this. No, nothing, listen, just jot down their names and surnames, they are going with us, there are no problems. Nothing is a secret any more. There are no secrets any more, so we are setting up unarmed detachments, we are organising, which means there is no need to keep a secret any more, but anybody suspect, any shady character, we should make a list of, because we have been told there are people who are suspect in the environs. Let me tell you one thing, as far as weapons are concerned, we have enough weapons. There are no problems on that score and we are now going to have to resort to training, so that people who come here are ready, you know. Now, how can we proceed further? What we are going to do, how are we going to do it? We have set up our detachments. We are going to set up a medical corps and strengthen our detachments in that way and we are going to have to have training courses. Of course, we will do this with the cooperation of MUP. You are going to go down to your departments now, take a look at the people and make a list of their names. Anybody who does not belong there -- we all know who does not belong there, but if they should be there, just make a note of this and I will tell them what the President said. Do not tell the people about arms. You will be able to tell them. We are forming unarmed detachments for such and such region and then you can line up -- we are going to line up and see the command posts in Bogdanovci up to Lustar and the bunker at Lustar which means this part, the Serbian part from here to Osijek, it is up to us to settle that situation -- other part will be settled by Osijek, and nobody is allowed to pass through here, so we cover all this area and we must link up the road from Bogdanovci to Lustar. We can do that, there are no problems there. Should everybody go or just the commanders? No, everybody."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: One question, please. Was that the time of the Croatian attack on the SFRY? May I have the following tapes? Was Croatia part of the SFRY at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We are hearing about the formation of unarmed detachments and detachments with arms, as far as I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, what is your answer? Mr. Fila asked you a question, whether --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer was in the affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to object, also, to the commentary offered by Mr. Fila just a moment ago. I did not catch it. I see it on the transcript. He said, "We are hearing about the formation of unarmed detachments and detachments with arms, as far as I can see." I think that is inappropriate to make that kind of comment. It is up to the court to assess the evidence and to determine what is there and for him to offer suggestions as to what the film shows, I think should be saved for argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila, I think the Prosecutor is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to say that it can be heard on the tape, the man saying that arms had been supplied, but I accept that. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If you need this at the decisive moment, organise two or three men for the liquidation. Yes, the physical liquidation. Yes. Dumb, dumb, dumb, our police does not dare. Does not dare? Yes, we go to somebody else and then somebody else at the same time. Those who are most dangerous can be killed at their door step, on their thresholds, no question asked, whether women, children, nothing is asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who is the gentleman that we can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Martin Spegelj, a former general of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who is he to kill at the threshold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All those who would be opposed to the break-up (INAUDIBLE), that is the officers of the Yugoslav Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In order to create which State?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The independent State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that period, was Croatia indisputably within the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, according to international law, it was, undeniably, part of Yugoslavia. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When did this take place, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was Croatia undeniably a part of Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In your diplomatic practice, did you ever hear or see that people can attack their official army, to take arms, to strangle soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. I was in America, where, had this occurred, everybody would have been arrested, if anybody were to attack a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This was the regular SFRY army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was Yugoslavia's regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was it attacked by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was attached by individuals of the Croatian nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May I see the next video clip? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is Bjelovar and the massacre of the members of the JNA. The JNA barracks in Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you tell us who the dead are, whose barracks they are, and who are the live ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are the barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army, their legal barracks. The killed individuals are killed officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, the legitimate army of Yugoslavia, and the perpetrators are the rebels, the Croatian paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that time, was Croatia a part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In September 1991, according to Croatian rule, Croatia was completely within the formation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I am sorry to interrupt you, but this is evidence we have already seen -- the films, we saw and the witness was not a witness to those particular facts -- he did not see them, so therefore I do not see the point of showing all those films which the court, as I say, has already seen and asking the witness about the facts, at which he was not present. I wonder whether you could expedite your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to understand each other in just a moment. You asked me the question of where I got those tapes from when I made my initial statement. I got them from the gentleman and they are part of the archives of the Museum of Genocide. That is why I am asking him what is on the films, to explain what I am showing and where I got the films from. As you know he was and is the director of the genocide in whose archives the films are contained. Therefore he can bear out the authenticity of the material presented -- it is not myself who made them or whatever. I am asking him in that sense. Do you understand me? May we see the next film and then we shall be completing this part of the evidence. Perhaps this is a good point for me to ask whether, at that period, other barracks -- JNA barracks were attacked -- I am asking for the period before 8 October 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, throughout Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia army barracks were attacked in the areas of Croatia. There were numerous cases of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was somebody blown up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a well-known case when a whole depot was blown up -- an arms depot.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we take a look at the film now? This film is dated 1991 and it is a film of Vukovar -- what the JNA found when it entered Vukovar; is that correct, Sir? Professor, would you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "..... In two streets alone, we counted several dozen massacred civilians. Was it good luck that saved Petar and Zuka Loncar, for they spent almost five months in their cellars. We can't go on living together; we have to separate from them. It's just not possible to live with them -- there is just no way. The guards, they killed us Serbs -- they massacred them when they saw that they were losing the war. You see the way they took their revenge. They are so furious. They don't know what to do, they fire at anything they see moving. They spared no-one. You can see them, they dug out people's eyes, cut off their ears, the most atrocious things. As you can see, this man was massacred with a bayonet. This happened perhaps three days ago. The man turned over on his stomach is Ilija Vukovic, that one used to be his house, that one that is in ruins. This other man, also on his stomach, he is the owner of this other house, he is also a Serb -- this woman that you see on top of the old woman is Ilija Vukovic's wife."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That would conclude our presentation of videotapes. This is all. I tender this into evidence -- the source is the Museum for Genocide, this is where I got the tapes from, and that would conclude what the Defence has to say regarding Vukovar in 1991, but let me just ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In relation to the tendering of the evidence, I realise that Mr. Fila's source was the Museum of Genocide, but I am wondering what the source was for the Museum of Genocide. With clarification of that, we would have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That is a good question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Well, that is the question. We will ask that question. You want to ask that question, is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I already said, we gathered in our video film centre in order to preserve the documents -- we gathered it from various sources, from various correspondents who were on site. We also received material from certain specialised services of the Yugoslav army which took footage on site from all the sources available to us. I travelled to Vukovar once myself to see this with my own eyes, because all those things that I have seen on film, and which you have seen here, it is impossible to imagine that such crimes happened. We realise that some things were correct, some things were incorrect, as happened for instance with the children -- this is something that was fascinating. An Italian journalist offered evidence, but without films, that 40 children were found all wrapped up, so to speak. I checked that one out and realised that it was not correct, so the credibility of those documents was -- they wanted to bring everything into question and the BBC refused to receive any documents from that area, from that time on. A mass of material here -- you cannot really check, but everything needs to be preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Defence has some false testimony here -- if you want to have a look at that, you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: That is -- let me ask the Prosecutor whether he is prepared to accept --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The film, we have no objection. We would have an objection to something which has already been characterised as false testimony coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So it is tendered in evidence and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We will be concluding shortly, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will be marked D40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When I submitted your expert report, the Tribunal asked from you in Belgrade to submit some books of yours. I do not know whether it was the Tribunal itself or the Office of the Prosecutor who requested that, but at any rate you submitted in book, did you not? Please have a look at it. (Handed). No, no, alright. I have only one copy, so I cannot tender this copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you tell us about this book, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to ask the expert witness to read out the title, because this is one of the books mentioned in the bibliography?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me answer -- the Office of the Observers of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia asked me to submit a number of books and articles of mine and of course I complied forthwith so that they can see what it was that I studied. This book is called, "The Break-up of the Yugoslav State 1991-1992, The Crime Against Peace -- The Responsibility of Vatican and Germany."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Unfortunately, I cannot tender this book, because this is an only copy. But the expert witness gave us a disk which contains the English translation of the book, so if it is necessary, the Defence is willing to provide you with this, because I do not need that. I would now like to ask our expert witness to have a look at those documents and to indicate where these are located in the book?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is marked Exhibit D41.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You speak both English and Serbian, so it will be easy for you to determine. (Handed). Will you please tell us at what location in this book are these excerpts from and what do they deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a chapter from the book in the Serbian version, it is page 286 and this is a translation of that chapter entitled, "Genscher and the Warning against Lord Carrington and the Secretary-General Perez de Cuellar: Genscher Rejects the Warning".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What is this document about -- when was it written and what is this about, in two sentences or so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In early December 1991, when I was carrying out my research in the United Nations, the tragedy of my people, since I have also served in New York as the Consul General of Yugoslavia, I came across some documents in which Lord Carrington, who was at the time the president or the chairman of the Conference on Yugoslavia, and the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Peres de Cuellar, wrote a letter to the Foreign Minister of the Federal Republic of Germany in which they warned him that an early recognition of the break-up of the Yugoslav State might have, as a consequence, a horrible tragedy of all the peoples in Yugoslavia. Genscher, who is one of the main architects of the break-up of the Yugoslav State, rejected in categorical terms the warnings by Lord Carrington and by the Secretary-General of the United Nations. In my opinion, that warning, and also from the historical distance that we have now, is extremely important, because, from that time on, all the statesmen recognised that. Unfortunately, it was too late for the peoples in Yugoslavia, that the early recognition of the break-up of Yugoslavia, before all the conditions were met to enable all the peoples there to have their rights recognised, that it was done in early December by Genscher -- after all the events in Vukovar, he rejected that warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said "refusal to recognise" -- the early recognition of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The early recognition of Croatia and Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So, I tender this into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like the witness to look at the next document. I apologise to the Prosecutor and to you, your Honours. Our witness is an expert in international law. He was the chief adviser in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and that is why I am using him for this purpose, as a source of information.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D42.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what this is about and at what location is this in your book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is on page 188 in my book -- this is about the role played by the European Community Troika, played by intervening in the internal affairs of the Yugoslav State by exerting pressure and insisting that the representative of Croatia, Stjepan Mesic, who at one stage openly said that he would break up the Yugoslav State and that this was his main purpose -- and that was of course the reason, as in any other State, that a man who wants to destroy a State cannot be at its head. However, the Troika of the European Community at that time, according to the transcripts which I had an opportunity to see, they guaranteed, including Mr. De Michaelis of Italy, that they would prefer the integrity of the Yugoslav State and they would force the secessionist States of Croatia and Slovenia not to secede by force, if certain constitutional procedures whereby they could secede from Yugoslavia and which the constitution envisaged, if they would be prepared to accept that, because any resorting to violence would result in serious consequences for the Yugoslav peoples. This is the essence of this and it is clear today that all those guarantees provided by the European Union were not respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please look at the following excerpt from your book. I would also like to tender this as evidence -- that is Defence Exhibit 43 and this is the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is Exhibit D42 and this one will be marked D43. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a chapter in my book. I have to note here --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Hold on a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to this coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Go ahead, please, what is this about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is about the responsibility of Germany, Austria and Hungary for the break-up of the Yugoslav State. This is located in my book which we have been discussing at page 134 and elsewhere. However, my edition, prepared for the world in the English language, differs in the presentation of the case, but the essence of the case is as follows: I would really like this to be understood, because this is a result of a study of the historical genesis of all this. All that happened inside Yugoslavia, you will admit, happens in all countries over the world. It happens in Italy, it happens in France, in many other States, and the tragedy of the Yugoslav peoples would not have occurred had it not been for the outside intervention. As you know, the UN Charter forbids this -- this is a crime against peace. Of course, there are some attempts at revisionism and I have the evidence for this -- the proof. I have always attempted in my research, as a combination of a legal expert and an historian, to establish facts. In this case, it is clear that there were some points in Germany where Croatian paramilitary forces were trained. We have concrete evidence that tens of thousands of Kalashnikovs were illegally imported from Hungary in contravention of the regulations for the purposes of paramilitary forces and in contravention of the JNA. The English edition would have been even broader than the Serbian edition. Had it not been for the intervention of the foreign forces, this tragedy of Yugoslav peoples would not have happened, there would have been negotiations and so forth but not a tragedy such as the one that happened. This is the purpose, to show the background of what happened in 1991 and 1992, where the roots lie, because all the crimes that we have been discussing today, these are the consequences. The fact is the basis that in 1941 the Yugoslav State was broken up, crimes of genocide occurred; in 1991 the second Yugoslav State was broken up and everything happened again. In the second Yugoslav State, you had the Greater Serbia, Greater Croatia, all the Muslims, they all lived together, but somebody did not like it and this had to be broken up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. In your research, did you come up with the fact that there were mercenaries in the Croatian armed forces, or in some other forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for the question. In 1995 I had the honour of visiting this esteemed Tribunal. I had a discussion with the deputy chief Prosecutor, Mr. Blewitt. I gave him a list of 13 mercenaries from this country, from The Netherlands, and I referred to the Convention on Mercenaries and I told him, according to my views of international law, these are the most harmful criminals who do not get any kind of international protection and I proposed that they be prosecuted and punished. This is where I saw the real purpose of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, and that list of 13 Dutch mercenaries was also submitted to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Netherlands pointing out to the Convention, signed by the Kingdom of The Netherlands and the Kingdom of Serbia, in 1895, and I proposed that certain measures be taken against those mercenaries. There are also mercenaries from Austria, Germany, from the United States, but, as far as I know, nothing was done -- they were not prosecuted, and what I as an expert in international law, and a person of international outlook, what I cannot see is how so many civilised countries, including the United States and The Netherlands, once those criminals are identified or gotten by them through an exchange, how they can fail to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, because the court might be interested in that, is the English version of the text here on this disk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this is the latest version dated 1996. I still continue my studies, I gather new documents and I have obtained some really significant documents. I have conducted my research in the Italian Foreign Ministry, in the general staff of the Italian army, in Kew Gardens archive in London, in the archives of the United States and France and of course all the archives in the former Yugoslavia which were accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to tender to this court on a disk. This contains the English version of the 400 pages of this book, so if somebody wants to have a look at it -- of course, if the Prosecution has no objection, I would like to tender this as evidence and, if not, as supporting material.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is D44.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Finally, I would like the last two documents to be admitted -- they have been admitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This does bring up one issue just now. Mr. Fila has mentioned something as supporting material -- if it is not tendered as evidence he would like to submit it as supporting material. We have not objected to this, it is finite would go in as to evidence. However, we want to make sure there is a clear understanding that anything that is submitted as supporting material is not being used as evidence for the decision of the court and just make sure there is no misunderstanding as to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This was just -- had you objected -- since you have no objections, everything is alright. The Defence has asked in the course of the trial and obtained from Belgrade a set of documents signed by the SFRY as international documents in the period from May 1991 until the end of 1991. Since our expert witness was a legal adviser to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, I would like these documents to be shown to him -- some are in French, some are in English, and some are in Serbian and if he can identify those documents for us, I think it would be useful in conjunction with the other documents. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D45.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like you to have a look at those documents separately and to tell us what are those documents -- what kind of documents are these?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first document is the Third Protocol on Financial Cooperation between the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and European Economic Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Dated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Brussels, 24 June 1990 -- 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second document, the coversheet for the World Bank, Japanese grant agreement dated 1991 between the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the International Bank for Restructuring and Development.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The date?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is there not a more exact date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I would say 4 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: October, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Protocol between the Socialist Executive Council of the SFRY and the Romanian Government on the Exchange of Goods and Services in 1991, signed 27 November 1991. The next one is a letter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, it is impossible to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was sent to Ambassador Mihiljica Jobrejnon, head of the Mission of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with the European Community in Brussels dated 18 September 1991. The next is a letter, cooperation -- it is probably a French title -- this letter was sent to the Yugoslav Ambassador Mihiljica Jobrejnon, and the last document is a verbal note from the US Embassy sent to the Federal Secretariat of Foreign Affairs of the SFRY, dated 25 June 1991, so that means immediately after the visit of the Secretary of State James Baker to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can it be said, since you are an expert in this area, that these documents refer to the sovereign State of SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the most formal documents, because they are agreements signed by States and exchange of notes, so this is the most official kind of communication between a State and international organs and other States.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does it mean the SFRY existed as a State?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Objection. That calls for a legal conclusion from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This witness is the chief legal adviser of the Minister of Foreign Affairs and he is making legal conclusions. I would like to tender this in to evidence as an exhibit and the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We would have no objection to it coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So we can move on to the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Dr. Bulajic, there were some other books as well that you have written that were not mentioned during the course of examination-in-chief. One of them is a book in which you have been rather critical of this institution, which is called "the alternative Yugoslavia Tribunal", which, on its cover, has a picture of a sword in the hand of the lady of justice here and it says "for Serbs" written on the sword. Is this the book that you published?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And in this book you said that the Security Council cannot establish an international court of law, and it is your conclusion that this is not really a court of law. Is that still your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I can explain if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My entire life I have been dealing with international law, especially United Nations law. I have cooperated with the International Court of Justice. My analyses on the setting up of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia were different than my express advocating of setting up an international criminal court of general jurisdiction for which I consider that the present-day mankind has need of. The setting up of individual courts for individual States, I do not see any reason absolutely for this and I should like to remind you that that is not only my own opinion, but it is the opinion of my distinguished colleague, whom I knew before he was the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Dr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali. His explanations at the very outset when this court was formed, but not to go into great length, you have had opportunities to see my book, I should like to give you my opinion. Every man is entitled to his own opinion, I think, with full respect for this Tribunal -- that is why I am here today, because I respect the Tribunal. If the Security Council is to create an international court on the basis of one legal premise, the right to create a subsidiary organ, according to my criteria, this cannot be how I envisage -- let me have my opinion -- how an International Tribunal should look like. I analysed and studied why the initiative of the United States was severed to set up an ad hoc court for Iraq, for Saddam Hussein, why did they give that idea up. Why was the Tribunal set up only for Yugoslavia and later on for Rwanda, which is a completely different case. Therefore, I would just like to state, and it is my own free opinion as a jurist, as somebody dealing in the law throughout my lifetime, I support the formation of an international criminal court, which will try all cases without limitation and that is why I should like also to express my deep respect of this Tribunal. I should like to remind you that, on one occasion, I put myself forward as amicus curiae to appear before this court and I discussed the matter with your officers and the gentleman in that representative officer, Mr. Mihov, so I would like to separate these two views, my opinion as a lawyer, as a jurist, as a legal man and why we are here today in the efforts of establishing the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You take issue in this book with the idea that individual responsibility should be the basis for prosecution of crimes at this time, saying rather that the forces responsible for the break-up of Yugoslavia is where you will find the roots of all the individual crimes and crimes of genocide. In the writings in at least the two books I have read you hold a number of people responsible for the break-up of Yugoslavia; Germany, the Vatican, Italy, Austria, Hungary, Croatia, Slovenia. I have not found anywhere in any of your books that you felt that Serbia had anything to do with the break-up of Yugoslavia; is that your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection. This is as interesting as Jasenovac is. I do not see the connection between his views on Germany and France and the reading of his books when I explained a moment ago that some 150,000 Serbs were killed in Jasenovac and the Germans do seem to have something to do with the trial here, so I do not think we should adhere to the theoretical opinions of what the gentleman wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this man is being put forward as an expert and the whole reason that experts are required to submit a list of their publications is so that they can be challenged on these to determine their credibility and perhaps their motivation for testifying. This man has made a lot of statements which relate directly to war crimes. I think they are relevant in determining his veracity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But still I wonder to what extent your question is relevant -- whether or not -- I wonder whether you could move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour, if you will note our objection. In this book, you include a number of articles that were written by other persons, as well, which seem to support your position and the views that you express; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What book are you discussing -- the same book?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The same book, "Alternative Yugoslavia Tribunal".

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Once again, an objection. I do not see what we are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: This is the book you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct. There are some other writings in here which I think certainly are relevant. This man is putting forth the view that there is no such thing as a war crime in this book. This is clearly relevant as to this man's credibility, when he is coming here and testifying about war crimes. If he is expressing a view first of all that this Tribunal does not exist, which he says is not a legal institution, is not really a valid court of law, all of this has to do with how much reliability should be placed on this gentleman's statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On the particular issue of his views -- the witness's views about the legality or credibility of our Tribunal, I think this -- he is entitled to hold any view about it, as a legal scholar, so I wondered to what extent it is relevant to us. If you want to pursue this matter on whether or not he speaks of war crimes, whether or not he believes that war crimes were committed, you may go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Very well, your Honour. In particular, there is an article written by a woman named Joan Phillips which is included in your book, which is entitled, "War Crimes: Myth and Reality". Do you agree with the conclusions that are reached in this article?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what sort of conclusions are reached in that article?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I was going to quote this directly. If he disagrees with it I did not see any reason to go into detail of what is in the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us allow the Prosecutor to move on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you agree with the conclusions reached in this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not agree with that conclusion. My attitude is very clear and principled. War crimes, crimes of genocide, regardless of the perpetrators, must be brought to a court of law for trial, regardless of whether we are dealing with Serbs, Croats, or Slovenes. That you have said there are other opinions in the book -- allow me to say that if we are going to constantly re-examine one's conclusions, we must listen to other people's views. On 13 April 1993, I initiated at my particular faculty, department, at my university, outside my official capacity, a round table meeting at which we asked the question of the setting up of an International Criminal Tribunal ad hoc for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do not go into this matter. Let us move on with other questions. This is not an issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Dr. Bulajic, you commented on this film that was shown to you about these armed detachments which were being formed, or in the case of Mr. Mercep, where he is talking about unarmed detachments and then, in the case of General Spegelj, the importation of arms. You said that this was not in accordance with SFRY law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was the formation of Serbian autonomous regions in accordance with SFRY law, or Croatian law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You probably saw in my biography my doctoral thesis was, "The Rights of Peoples to Self-Determination". Later on it was confirmed in the UN that this is one of the basic principles of international modern law. If Croatia at that time forcibly separated, contrary to the rights and regulations of the Yugoslav constitution and constitutional law in general, the same right was enjoyed by the Serbian people from the aspects of the rights of self-determination, because it was contrary to the so-called Austro-Hungarian theory of State law. Let me remind you of a precedent of West Virginia during the secessionist war in the US when the State of Virginia had joined the Confederation and West Virginia opted for the union and today in the constitution of the US there are two States, you have Virginia and you have West Virginia. Therefore, when we are breaking up Yugoslavia and when the constitution of Yugoslavia is not being respected, if one peoples refer to the right to self-determination, then the same right applies to another peoples, especially as, according to the Croatian constitution, the Serbian people are a constituent peoples who fought in the course of the Second World War for its right in that country and was recognised at the time of Hungary and so on and so forth, not to go back to history too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You did not really answer my question. You said because Croatia did it, then the Serbs should do it, but my question was specifically, was this in violation of the SFRY law? It is a very simple question -- "Yes" or "No", was it a violation and then, if you need to explain, please do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not in violation of the Yugoslav constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The film that was shown about the attack on the barracks in Bjelovar, which was entitled, "The Massacre of the JNA Soldiers at Bjelovar", this occurred at the end of September, did it not -- I believe it was 29 September 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly what the date was, but at that time, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And this was already well after the JNA forces were engaged in battle with Croatian forces in Vukovar, for example, which had started at least a month earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand what you have in mind -- the Yugoslav army -- it was the legal army of Yugoslavia performing its constitutional duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think the question was rather simple. This was a month after the Yugoslav army had begun engaging in battle with Croatian forces in the town of Vukovar, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly the time that the Yugoslav army was engaged. I do not know that, but I can say that it was within the frameworks of the legal functions of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And this was at least during a state of armed conflict between the forces of the Yugoslav army and the Croatian authorities; correct -- Croatian military forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not Croatian military authorities; they were insurgent authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you at least agree that there was a state of armed conflict between the JNA and somebody from the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course -- the armed conflict unfortunately did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And is it not a fact that there were a number of JNA barracks spread throughout Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not a great number or a small number -- it was as it was prescribed by Yugoslav army formations. There were no special barracks or new barracks. They were the barracks that had existed for many years -- for decades, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The JNA soldiers that were in the vast majority of these barracks left Croatia peacefully without harm; is that not correct, in organised convoys into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether they left as peacefully as you say -- where conditions existed for this, they probably did, but the fact was there was a rebellion going on and there were separate plans elaborated of cutting off water and electricity, creating blockades and special military facilities to stop the legal army from functioning on the territory of its own State.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: In fact, in Bjelovar, the JNA commander had resisted requests for him to abandon the garrison and to leave and had begun firing on the town of Bjelovar, had he not, and there was a return of fire and in fact there was a battle over the barracks in Bjelovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What would any other honourable officer do in any army in the world but react in that way -- what would you have him do?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I apologise, your Honours. I did not understand properly. At whose demand was the commander of the Bjelovar -- when did he refuse to do this? At whose demand, at whose request -- at the request of which State -- the representative of what State? What demand -- what are you talking about exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I think it has been very clear, that the Croats asked the soldiers to leave, asked the officers to abandon the garrison, that in this situation the JNA forces fought, a battle ensued, and this is where the deaths occurred, during the course of this battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Once again, I apologise, your Honours, what Croats -- Croats are a nation, there are children, the elderly, women, physicians, engineers -- which Croats -- Croats as a nation cannot pose requests of this kind, so who tabled this request for the legal SFR army to leave Yugoslav territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The Croatian Government, but I believe he has already answered the question. You mentioned this fact about an Italian journalist offered evidence about 40 children killed and that this was not true. Is it not a fact that she was given this information by the JNA -- she reported it, Reuters ran it all over the world and then, when she insisted on seeing the bodies, the JNA finally admitted that this was a false report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally researched this case -- in all my researches and the book that we offer on the children of the victims of genocide -- the crime of genocide is the greatest crime, crimes against children are the worst of these crimes and when I heard about this news item, that 40 children had been killed, that they were in a group and that they were packed like rubbish in small plastic bags, truly, as a father, as a man, I could not believe this, because anybody who had perpetrated such a crime I do not think we should go into research of this kind. I checked with the Yugoslav People's Army, with the most competent authorities, the head of the legal department who was my colleague, who was on the spot, on the location, and confirmed what I learned. I went to Vukovar personally, I was brought a "witness" -- a alleged witness -- an alleged eye witness. I asked for a meeting with him, I met him. "Let me have some proof", I said. But nobody brought any proof, although this was a source from the Yugoslav People's Army and a source in favour of the Serbs. I said, "No, that is not true, and any untruths should be condemned." Therefore, there was no different opinion in the Yugoslav People's Army and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I do not think there is any dispute that the information was false. We all agree with that. My question to you, though, was that this Italian journalist did not just originate this story on her own. She received the story from the JNA, did she not, in the first place -- "Yes" or "No", and then explain as needed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Yes" or "No" in what sense, tell me -- no, because she did not get it from the JNA -- that is my answer -- my answer is "No" in that sense. How she arrived at that particular piece of information -- her.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I have the tape. If you want to know where false information comes from, we can show the tape and the Prosecutor will no doubt be satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I do not think we need to see this tape. Does the Prosecution want to see the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No, your Honour. You have indicated there were mercenaries in the Croatian army. Is it your position that there were none in the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not my position -- probably there was among the Serbs, too, but my attitude is clear-cut -- mercenaries are the most terrible crime according to international law -- anybody who is paid to kill anybody, that is the worst possible crime, according to international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You talk about Serb homes being burned in areas of Croatia, and Serbs being forced out. Is it not true that Croats were forced out from Serb areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly -- probably there were cases of that kind, too. Unfortunately, action leads to reaction. One hostile action leads to another hostile action and I do not say that any type of cleansing is alright. What I was particularly affected by was where war conflicts break out one can understand a lot of things, but in areas where there were no armed conflicts, for example, the Croatian region of Goske Kotar, houses were burned, people killed. People were loyal citizens there -- there were no barricades, nothing of that kind in the area, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You have also written another book about the role of the Vatican in the break-up of the Yugoslav State and you seem to hold the Pope responsible for much of what happened in Yugoslavia -- is that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With full respect for his Honour, the Pope, I do hold him responsible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you talk about -- you refer to the Tudjman Government as an Ustashi Government; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I used the word "Ustashi", but pro Ustashi quite definitely, because it was a continuation of the policy -- that is evident. The historian himself, the actual President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, publicly and expressly stated that the Ustashi independent State of Croatia was an expression of the age-old historical traditions and aspirations of the Croatian people, and the commander of the Jasenovac camp in Buenos Aires was visited by Dr. Tudjman. He expressed his recognition and Vinko Vinkovic, one of the SABOR members, was a member of the Ustashi genocide, he was included into the SABOR Croatian Parliament, not to mention other cases of continuity. He took away the Serbs' right as a constituent people. He does not allow Serbs to return to Croatia today. He organised the Muslim supreme commander of the Storm drive, and the other drive where hundreds of thousands of people were made to flee, so the Serbian people no longer represent a constituent people but neither are they are a minority and this means that the plan to genocidally exterminate the Serbs, which was started by Pavelic has succeeded. If you read anti-Semitism in the Pathless Roads and other works, I think the whole situation will become clear to you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Dr. Tudjman's book, he was quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You state in your book "Alternative Yugoslavia Tribunal" that the right of one people must not overrule the rights of other peoples. You would maintain, I assume, that the Serbs have followed this principle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are first raising a principled question, a question of principle, and that is quite right, but I do not say that in the name of the Serbian people but as an internationalist for every nation in the world and for all the Yugoslav nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But, again, my question is, do you believe that the Serbs have followed that policy in Yugoslavia, that they have respected the rights of others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know who you have in mind when you say "the Serbs" -- the Serbs like myself, the Serbian Government, the Yugoslav Government did follow that principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No questions. I shall try and read the book by Dr. Tudjman myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume there is no objection to the witness being released? Dr. Bulajic, thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may be released. We stand adjourned for 15 minutes. (11.55 a.m.) (A short break) (12.13 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Before we start, may I discuss a matter with both parties? There is a matter about the organisation of our future work. I understand from the Registrar that it will be more convenient and technically possible to establish the video link on 25 May instead of 18 May -- it will be much better. I wonder whether you are going to call a sufficient number of witnesses for the previous week, the 18th to the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As it is half a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, we have half a day. Do you have, right now, a rough idea how many witnesses you will call in May? We know that 12 are to be heard via video link, but I understand you have reduced the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, there will be fewer people. Your Honours, I will try and get some new witnesses to clarify some military matters over the army, but 23 or 24 witnesses, but they will all be very quick, because they will be on the link, they are individuals on tape for the most part, and as I said at the beginning, we are first going to get through the expert witnesses, the general situation in Vukovar in 1990 and 1991 and then to the others. I am beginning this with this particular witness. I think it will be fairly quick and I hope that you do not have any objections and criticisms of my speed today, except for the way I talk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Again, how many witnesses are you going to call through video links?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: About 20 -- a video conference, about eight -- the video link, about eight witnesses -- there seems to be the need for -- we receive new data every day, so we do not have to have two or three witnesses, we can reduce the number, the number is being reduced. But, as I said earlier on, I shall be completing this in May, that is for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness is Mr. Novakovic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. LJUBOMIR NOVAKOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, did you conduct a talk with inspector Vasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions he took down a statement and a supplementary statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you take a look at this statement and say if it was the one that you made?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is marked D46, English translation 46A.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It exists in Serbian and English. (Handed). Will you have a look at this document and tell us whether it is your supplementary statement. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my statement, yes. The statement I made to Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not received the supplement yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D47.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a statement in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The translation is here in Serbian. That is the statement in Serbian, a supplementary statement in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be D47 and the English translation is D47A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my statement in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If there are no objections, may this be tendered as D46 and D47?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, were you the President of the Municipal Assembly of Backa Palanka from 1989 to 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was from the end of 1989 to the end of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where is Backa Palanka located in relation to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Backa Palanka is on the left-hand side of the Danube and Ilok is on the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What are the links between Backa Palanka and Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The communications between Backa Palanka and Ilok were great, cultural sports and cultural relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Physically was there a bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a bridge which was built up in 1974 during Tito's reign.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During the war events of 1991, the second half of 1991, how did you traverse the bridge; could you cross the bridge freely, or did you need a permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On both sides, the military authorities issued permits, both the Republic of Serbia and the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What military authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military authorities that existed in Yugoslavia, whereas the other side had their own authorities, which gave permission for the community of Ilok to be able to go to Backa Palanka to work -- they were employed in Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At that time, did people leave Ilok towards Backa Palanka and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were a fair number of mixed marriages -- there were Slovaks and Croats and they wanted to move to Yugoslavia and we allowed this relocation to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know that the population of Ilok went over on -- that is, 17 October 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these people, in keeping with the referendum in Ilok, those who wanted to stay in Ilok and those who wanted to move out -- in conformity with the military authorities, and civilian authorities, that took part in the negotiations, by referendum, most people said that they wanted to move towards the interior of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you show the witness now Prosecutor's exhibit number 5, it is the agreement on Ilok between -- while we are looking for that, you know that there was mediation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the European Community and the United Nations and the people of Ilok and on the other side Colonel Grahovac and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you say "army", because there are several armies would you please use the term "the Yugoslav People's Army" or "the Croatian army"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the Yugoslav People's Army, which existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the introductory part and who this was signed by (Handed). Would you read it out aloud?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "On the basis of a request by the inhabitants of Ilok and the referendum, all citizens are enabled from these settlements, as refugees, who commanded be allowed to leave this locality with members of their family. Number 2."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who is the signatory of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mate Brletic on the one side and colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army, Petar Grahovac on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you look at page number 1 and the introduction at the top -- could you read it clearly so that we can understand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The military commander of the units of the JNA in Sid, represented by Major General Dragolub Arsenijevic, or Arandelovic" -- I cannot quite see -- "and the representative of Ilok and Sarengrad, Mrsic Ivan as the mayor and Brletic Mate, as head of the police station in Ilok, Kraljevic Stipan, the President of the negotiating committee, and present were representatives of the European mission --" This is in English, "Hugo and Peter": "-- on 14 October in Sid." Will you tell us what that agreement represents -- what was the referendum, who requested permission to move out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not have to move out, but the local authorities of Ilok wanted to sound the opinion of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On what question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the peaceful relocation of people towards the interior of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were they coerced into this, were they made to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you in any way take part in these negotiations -- were you present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As they were all my friends from Ilok and remain my friends and as they believed in me as a pacifist and as somebody who did a lot for Ilok's development, they asked me to attend these talks with their leadership where the agreement was in fact reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: During those talks, did some -- did anybody insist the population of Ilok should leave Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the referendum, what were the questions asked at the referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question was, "Who wishes to remain in Ilok and who wishes to move to Croatia?"

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the people wishing to remain, what would they have to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing -- to live normally like all the other citizens in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And to surrender their arms, of course, I hope?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to avoid armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Slavko Dokmanovic take part in those negotiations in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The SFRJ, that is what we are talking about, would you please refer to it as the SFRJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know that Mr. Mesic and others left the SFRY in August of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It says SRJ and the correct title is SFRJ for the records, please, thank you. Since when have you known Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known him from 1990. As he was the President of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar, I was the mayor of Backa Palanka, and as they are two neighbouring towns and as we were all as cooperating economically culturally and in the sports field, we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How far did you -- until when did you cooperate with him as the President of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1990, after the Croatian extremists forbid coming to Vukovar, the Croatian Government took a decision to dissolve their assembly, and Marin Vidic -- Bili -- was appointed as some sort of executive president.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were you sure that was in 1990 and not 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was in 1990 -- 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the attempts of Slavko Dokmanovic to solve conflicts peaceably? Was he in favour of having issues between Croats and Serbs settled peaceably in the Vukovar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Honourable court, I can say this, and this can be attested by both the television cameras of Zagreb and Belgrade, that Slavko was a pacifist and humanitarian and always sought to resolve problems peaceably, to retain Yugoslavia, Backa Palanka and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he have any problems with this, with certain extremist Serbs, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was precisely condemned by the Serb extremists, because he always opted for a peaceful option and wanted to have everybody stay in his own region and to live in a common State. He encountered most of his problems with the Serbs, because they even asked for his physical liquidation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1991, what functions did he perform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was Minister of Agriculture -- as he was a great expert in agriculture, he was the most distinguished and highly regarded expert for the crop of rape, and he was there to organise production, to sow and harvest the crops properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have any cooperation in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, he came for combine harvesters and fuel, to be able to deal with the harvest on time; particularly as that was a very rainy year, we had to work efficiently and quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you see him on 16 and 17 October in Ilok, in Backa Palanka -- that was when Ilok was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zdenko Vodicka, who on the 16th in the morning, came to me and asked me to call Slavko, because on the 17th he did not want to resettle or move to Croatia -- I informed him, he came to me on the 16th and he thought that it was on the 16th that he was to help Zdenko and I said no, this was tomorrow, the moving was to take place tomorrow, and on the 17th, Slavko came with Rade Leskovac, we went in the afternoon hours to the bridge on the Ilok side and from that column we took over Zdenko Vodicka, who crossed by car and we came to Backa Palanka and they went off towards Trpinja and his wife remained in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the only reason why Slavko Dokmanovic came to Ilok, to help Zlatko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because they were great friends and have remained great friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On 20 November 1991, did some individuals come to your office and who were these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 20 November, the President of the Municipal Assembly of Kladovo came to me and he also came for economic cooperation among certain companies and firms. He came to my office and afterwards Jovo Cvetkovic, the President of the Jagodina Municipality and of Ursac, Dragoslav Aleksic came as well, and Slavko came to my office as well, and of course there was the journalist from Kladovo, who filmed all this -- filmed the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this an official meeting or an informal more or less friendly meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A friendly meeting in my office, so that we could meet, and they then left for Vukovar, and they were given permits to be able to cross the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could they cross the bridge otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, permits were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Slavko Dokmanovic have an official post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was just in the sphere of agriculture, within the Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It will be interesting to know how you recall that this was exactly on 20 November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because -- from my agenda, where I made a note of all my meetings, and when Slavko was arrested, I had a look to see what happened -- the events as they happened, and, once I retire, I wanted to do some writing, and I saw that he had visited me precisely on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Before I show you the tape, your Honours, I am going to go on to identify what Slavko Dokmanovic was wearing, according to our civil law system, and the witness can explain this -- describe it. Will you -- can you recall 20 November 1991? What was Slavko Dokmanovic wearing on that day? I know that a lot of time has gone by -- many years have gone by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did not have water and electricity, so he was wearing a hunting uniform, which did not have to be washed like other clothing, as often as other clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And did you have any electricity and water in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was the situation the same as Vukovar, are they two States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are two States now, but not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I conclude that, if there is water in Backa Palanka and electricity, the same does not apply to Trpinja and Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There could not have been any water supply or electricity, because the electrical system had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: May I now have a look at the tape? Before we look at the tape, I should like to show the witness the clothing worn by Slavko Dokmanovic and ask whether that is the particular clothing that he saw him wearing. This would be a Defence exhibit. It is composed of three parts -- a shirt and the rest. Would you please show it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is marked as D48.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you take the items out one by one, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the witness says anything, I just want to be sure, are you saying, as the Defence, that those are the clothes he wore, or that those clothes are similar to what Dokmanovic was wearing on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we maintain that that is exactly the clothing -- that particular clothing is what he was wearing on that particular day -- not similar but that clothing precisely -- original clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can see that it is hunting clothing, this is where the bullets go, hunter's keep their bullets, and it was good protection for health reasons. This was the shirt worn underneath -- this came on top, and then followed by this vest, and the trousers -- you can look at the size and everything else -- it is hunting trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You were there for a long time and you had contacts with the army. Does a uniform of the Yugoslav People's Army of this kind exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can we then conclude this is what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a hunting suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should like to tender this as Defence Exhibit 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should now like to ask us to play the tape for the witness. Your Honours, he is at the very start of the tape, because he did not go to Vukovar later, so it is a very brief tape -- I do not want to tire you with too many videotapes today, and would the witness say that he recognises his own appearance when he appears -- could he tell us that it is himself appearing. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That was on 20 November at 8.37.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Backa Palanka, the Municipal Assembly. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: They have the town -- this costs 50 kilos of bullets, 2,000 marks. I have two certificates for the first four years of primary school. That is Backa Palanka."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not on the tape yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you will show us when you appear on the tape, please. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The date of birth, the place of birth, I love freedom -- that is the first inscription. The second is 'I love Marija' -- 'I love you Marija'. Pezerovic Zeljko, Celarevo with the telephone number, that is the address."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is me, I am smoking a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would now like to show the witness some photographs -- that is the photograph of the witness on the tape, and we can carry on with the tape, so that you can see when this photograph occurs on the tape -- this image. This is a still of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When that still turns up, would you please tell us? (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we are, that is it -- that is the still, the one I showed you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could your voice be heard on the tape previous to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Will you tell us some of the individuals, their names, who appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Nebojsa Lazarevic, I saw Jova Cvetkovic and the one that took the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I should like to ask you something else. Did you see Slavko Dokmanovic wearing this uniform earlier on, on some other occasion, in the course of these months -- did he wear anything else -- anything different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him wearing this uniform, this hunting suit, during the harvest and sometimes he wore jeans, when it was warmer -- when the weather was warmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my examination of the witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, what was Nebojsa Lazarevic wearing on 20 November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago -- sometimes he was dressed in a sports manner and sometimes he wore a tie -- he was a rather elegant man, so he would wear a tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What about Mr. Cvetkovic, what was he wearing on 20 November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As he was a deputy with me, he was always nicely dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you be a little more specific? What colour clothing was he wearing on that day, can you describe it in the same detail that you have described Mr. Dokmanovic's clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you must understand that seven or eight years have elapsed since that time -- Slavko was always characteristically dressed -- because there was no water and electricity, he usually wore the hunting suit that we saw -- but my recollections, my memory -- I do not know if I saw it on tape, because a lot of time has gone by -- I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The noise is not a problem for the court or for the court reporters or anything?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It seems to be a problem with the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Why do we not move on in the hope that they will have stopped?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, how often did you see Slavko Dokmanovic during the course of the battle in Vukovar, during the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not want to talk about the battle -- I want to talk about the matters that I dealt with, with Slavko, concerning the harvest, and tractors, fuel -- combine harvesters -- that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am asking you -- I mention the battle as a time frame, the autumn of 1991, how often did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whenever he had me to come, he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: How often was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would have to look at my personal papers that I keep -- I said that at the beginning -- I would have to look at my agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Can you say is this once, twice, five times, 20 times -- I mean, you should have some idea how often you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite a few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you recall meeting with an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor, a Mr. Kevin Curtis, on 20 February this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that they visited me, but they had not announced themselves and they were very fair and I wish that this Tribunal would remain as fair as they were with me, until the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you recall telling Mr. Curtis that you saw Slavko Dokmanovic on a regular basis, pretty much every other day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had said that he saw me as often as he needed, which was quite a few times, so I would have to go through my agenda to count all those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you have your agenda in court here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had not brought my agenda, because nobody had told me it would be necessary, but I can bring it, whenever you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Why was there such frequent contact between you and Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you have to be aware of the fact that we had become good friends when he was the president of the municipality and also he constantly needed assistance for agriculture, because, after the summer harvest, there was the work that needed to be done in the fields during the autumn, and for that you also needed all the machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And, as president of the municipality, were you commonly referred to as the mayor of Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I am not the mayor; I am the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
