utterances.text: And were you ever commonly referred to as the mayor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Since according to our statute on the local self-government, it says the president of the Municipal Assembly and together with the 41 assembly men, he has equal rights as all of them and he only authorises the Executive Council. That is the only role that he has -- the only specific role that he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I assume the same would be true for Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time period that you are asking me about, he was not the president of the Municipal Assembly -- he was the Minister of Agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But, previously, when he had been the president of the municipality, the same would be true then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that in Croatia they had the same law on self-government -- every Republic had its own specific rules regarding the local self-government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Throughout your discussions with Mr. Curtis, you do not recall referring to Mr. Dokmanovic as the mayor of Vukovar throughout that entire talk, and also referring to yourself as the mayor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not a mayor -- you can check our law on self-government and local administration in Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that you had water and electricity in Backa Palanka -- this was throughout the course of the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Backa Palanka always had water and electricity supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you said that -- you were seeing Mr. Dokmanovic on a regular basis. Did you notice any particular odour associated with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you could feel the smell of sweat, the hunting uniform did give off -- I do not know how to explain this -- but it was the smell of sweat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You were a good friend of Mr. Dokmanovic's, would you not say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am still his friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And, during this entire two- or three-month period, on all of his visits to Backa Palanka, he never asked you if he could take a bath or perhaps wash some clothes, or do something like that in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did offer that to him, but he refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You said that you had electricity and water in Backa Palanka. Was it not true that Backa Palanka also provided water and electricity to Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ilok and several villages around Ilok, they did receive electricity from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you responsible for the blackout of electricity for five days to Ilok in September, to put pressure on the people there to move?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because it was not in my jurisdiction -- this was up to the power supply company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Why was electric power maintained in Backa Palanka but was cut off to Ilok -- who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That decision was not made by anyone. You have to be aware of the fact that electricity can be cut off when there is a severe thunderstorm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But if you have electricity in Ilok -- sorry, in Backa Palanka, but you do not have it in Ilok for five days and you have the same source of electricity, where did the problem come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that fact that Ilok's electricity supply was cut off -- I cannot accept that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the supply of yeast being cut off to Ilok, thus making it impossible for them to make bread?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know that they did not have electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Could you explain perhaps why several thousand people would just decide out of the clear blue to abandon their homes and move to some other place if there was no pressure put on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no pressure and the referendum proves that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So you think this was a free vote, that several thousand people would just decide to leave their homes that they had built or owned and just move away with their belongings that they can take in a car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You can check that with the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But I am asking you, why would several thousand people do this, out of the clear blue, if there was no pressure put on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am asking you -- why did many Serbs and Slovaks and others, as well as honest Croats, why did they move out voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Would you answer my question? Why did several thousand people leave Ilok if there was no pressure put on them -- it is a very simple question. I understand there was a referendum, but why did they choose to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they wanted to be closer to their matrix country.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: They were in their matrix country, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the referendum tells you everything. They were afraid of the war, just as we were in Backa Palanka -- we were in the same position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, what happened to the people in Lovas, Babska, Trvarjni, Sarengrad, Movo and Sotinj -- all those Croatian villages, all those people who had come to Ilok, you do not think that in any way affected their decision to move?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about that -- you will have to ask that from the people in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: What about an ultimatum that was given to the people of Babska which came about as part of the same negotiations over Ilok in which the JNA threatened to flatten the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I do not know anything about that fact and it is outside of my competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: So, just to conclude this, it is your contention that the people in Ilok left there totally voluntarily, gave up their homes and moved just because they wanted to be somewhere else. There was no pressure exerted on them whatsoever, by the JNA or by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they left, many still went to work to Backa Palanka and many still do, until this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you have indicated that the reason for Mr. Dokmanovic being on the bridge on 17 October was that he had come there because of his friend, Zlatko Vodicka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is contrary to what you had told Mr. Curtis, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, what I am saying now is the truth, and it can be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fail to understand as regards what this witness was saying to Mr. Curtis -- has this been tendered into evidence? Can I see that, or is this again some story containing assertions? I have insisted several times. For instance, I asked Dr. Bosanac, why did Serbs come out of Vukovar, she told me to ask the Serbs. Now I have asked the Serbs and you have heard what they have said but I was not talking about what was said to somebody else. Who is this man Curtis, what were they talking about and what is the basis for the Prosecutor claiming that this witness had said something else before? I have not seen this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: This is entirely appropriate cross-examination. This man has given a statement to the Prosecutor. I have notes based on that and I am questioning him on it. He has the opportunity either to confirm it or deny it and then, during the course of our rebuttal case, if he has denied this, we will be happy to put on Mr. Curtis to testify under oath as to exactly what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: May I ask you what you have got from Mr. Curtis -- notes or a statement signed by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have notes, not a signed statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Notes by Mr. Curtis?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, I think you can go on asking questions to the witness about what he said to Mr. Curtis, provided that afterwards you can produce him as a rebuttal witness to contradict --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Mr. Fila would have ample opportunity to cross-examine him, to question him on anything that he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You may go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you remember telling Mr. Curtis that the reason that Slavko Dokmanovic was on the bridge at Ilok on 17 October was that you and he were both there to ensure that everything went smoothly, and that you had been authorised to be there by your assembly, and that Slavko had been authorised, because he was the Minister of Agriculture, and he still felt as if he were the mayor of his municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding this investigation you are talking about, I only speak my native language -- I do not know what has been written down, because I have not signed anything. It would be fair of you to let me read this and sign it. I told you why Slavko was there -- to get Mr. Vojdicka out, because Mr. Vojdicka wanted to go to Trpinja because his wife stayed behind in Vukovar. I think I was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was there an interpreter present when Mr. Curtis was speaking with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a girl, a woman -- I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Was there a recruiting office for the Territorial Defences in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was within the jurisdiction of the Serbian Territorial Defence -- it is not in the jurisdiction of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But I am asking was there a recruiting office for the Territorial Defence geographically located in Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The recruiting centre for our district was in Novi Sad. They only have two -- an office with two officials in our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Dokmanovic was very moderate -- a pacifist, a great humanitarian who sought to retain Yugoslavia. Were you aware of his activities with the Serbian National Council as early as January 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of the fact and I still maintain that Slavko still thinks that it would have been best if Yugoslavia had remained whole and he is a pacifist -- proof of that is the fact that his own people wanted to liquidate him, because he was such a great Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Were you familiar with this group, "the Serb National Council"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not really -- only what I learned from the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Do you recall telling Mr. Curtis that you felt that since you still considered Slavko Dokmanovic the president of the municipality, you thought it was important to keep him informed about what was going on in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in May, he left that post -- actually, he was removed forcibly, but since he was still the Minister of Agriculture, since this was his native region and his municipality, he liked to hear what was going on, and many from the Ilok leadership met with Slavko, because they thought him to be a great man, and the man who was the most popular person in that region in the times of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You told Mr. Curtis, I believe, that Mr. Dokmanovic was very upset about the destruction in Vukovar and even broke down in tears -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. When we talked in private, he cried many times, because he could not believe that Vukovar could look what it looks like, because the provocations came first from the Ustashi and you know what happened in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And you also said that he felt great rage against Mercep, Seks and Glavas as the persons responsible for what happened in Vukovar; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that this Tribunal has the information and this can be verified through the European Community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you answer this question -- this is whether you remember saying all that, that you felt great rage against Mercep -- this is the question put by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am sorry, it was not that he felt great rage, that Mr. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that we did mention those three names -- because everybody knew what their nationalist views were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: And do you recall if he expressed rage at them as being the persons responsible for what had happened in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian people know this best, and the local Croats and Slovaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: You still have not answered my question, Mr. Novakovic. This is the third time I have put it to you: do you recall if Mr. Dokmanovic expressed rage at these people as the ones responsible for the destruction of Vukovar -- "Yes" or "No", and then explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, he felt it and I still feel that they are the most responsible, by doing what they did in May -- those three persons -- and they were at the forefront during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: If they were the ones responsible and this was just a response from the Serbs, why was it necessary for all the Croatian people to leave that region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, it is not true that all the Croats had left. You can verify that through the European Community -- they have the exact number of people who had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, are you telling this court that the vast majority of Croatian people did not leave the region of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, a part of them did leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: A part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just as a part of Serbs did leave Slavonia and Baranja and came to Backa Palanka, Sombor, Odzak, Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection. He insists on the witness giving him the answer he wants. He said "a part of Croats" and that should be enough. The Prosecutor is arguing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like those notes. If you see that somebody is using something before this court, and as far as I know, in the Anglo-Saxon law, those notes should be shown and translated in order for them to be used, because they are being used before this court and they are non-existent. What if Mr. Curtis fails to testify tomorrow? As far as I know, that is the came Mr. Curtis who lied to Mr. Dokmanovic that he would be able to go back safely, so that is the man who lied once before. He guaranteed Dokmanovic safety and lured him into Croatia, and he stated before this Tribunal that he had used deception to get close to Dokmanovic and to have him arrested, if that is the same gentleman, and I would have to see those notes in order to verify their existence, if they are indeed being used before this Tribunal. I am just asking a legal question. What if Mr. Curtis failed to testify? Then what is the basis for the questioning of this witness? I want to see those notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: A question of failure to testify is a matter which we would deal with appropriately at the time. These notes are notes which were taken down and given to the Prosecutor for the purposes of examining witnesses who were going to be called by the Defence. At the end of the day it is incumbent on the Prosecution to call the witness and to have the witness attest to these matters. There is no obligation under the Rules to produce notes -- notes are a matter of work product. They are not matters which are discoverable under the Rules and, your Honours, at the end of the day, if there are any notes made by the witness, which he would rely upon for the purpose of his testimony, the appropriate time is then for Mr. Fila to call for them and say, "I want to inspect those notes," and then they can be made available at that stage. It is inappropriate at the moment to be asking for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fila, have you got any questions in re-examination of your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, I would just like the witness to have a look at the notes and to tell us what those notes are. I keep saying that these notes do not exist. I do not know who those notes belong to -- until I have seen them. I got my name according -- I was named after Saint Thomas and he did not believe until he saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, we have just heard from the Prosecutor that the notes do exist but the Prosecutor has no duty to produce them in court. You do not have any questions for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you help us with this -- the meeting on 20 November, we saw the video of it. What was the meeting about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the guests arrived and since they had probably arranged that with Slavko, they had their own agenda or programme, where they went, they went across with the permit of the military authorities, we had coffee at my place, we discussed what the situation was, what was going to happen later, and whether any assistance was needed to repair things -- since there was a lot of destruction in the agricultural field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have a question. Is it correct to say that Ilok was under the jurisdiction of the regional government for the District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that, whether it was under their jurisdiction, but I assume that, at that time, the Croatian authorities held that part of Ilok, Sarengrad and Babska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You met Mr. Dokmanovic on 17 October 1991. Was he wearing the hunting suit, or a normal civilian suit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was wearing the hunting clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there is no objection to the witness being released, so thank you for coming here to give evidence. You may be released. We stand adjourned until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to thank you, too. (The witness withdrew) (At 1.15 p.m. the matter adjourned until Tuesday, 28 April 1998, at 8.30am) 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
